summary:
Farlight is a citizen science platform providing a user-friendly environment for investigating actual infrared observations collected by NASA SPHEREx project and observe how the sky changes over time. In the Farlight interface, users can choose a region of the sky, access its available observations, and compare images across different visits and wavelengths to look for interesting changes or objects.

In addition, Farlight makes it much more appealing by offering an interactive environment where the user can use not only visualize but also use scientific analysis tools, annotation tools and a workspace to record their findings. This makes it possible for people to be actively involved in exploring astronomical data rather than simply viewing it.

Farlight also aims to make this activity less intimidating through an AI Discovery Companion that can explain observations, help users investigate their own questions and guide them through the available evidence. the purpose of using AI here is not to make it announce any discoveries, but to give people better tools to make them themselves. By making genuine scientific data more accessible and understandable, Farlight hopes to encourage curiosity and meaningful public participation in astronomy.

(In the current hosted demonstration, the AI assistant is not enabled because its API key has not been configured.)
details:
Farlight – Exploring the Universe Through Real SPHEREx Data

Farlight is an interactive citizen-science platform that makes real observations from NASA's SPHEREx infrared space telescope accessible for exploration and analysis. It allows users to investigate astronomical fields, compare observations from different visits, examine infrared wavelength bands, and identify changes or potential transient sources in the sky.

The platform retrieves publicly available SPHEREx observational data and processes it through a scientific pipeline. Users can explore individual image frames, compare visits, generate difference images, adjust image visualisation parameters, and inspect measurements and candidate detections. The pipeline incorporates background estimation, image alignment, resampling, covariance-aware uncertainty propagation, and source detection. Field-specific information and processing provenance help users understand where the data comes from and how the results were obtained.

A key benefit of Farlight is that it lowers the barrier to working with genuine astronomical datasets. Instead of requiring specialised astronomy software or extensive knowledge of scientific data formats, users can explore observations through an accessible web interface. It also encourages scientific literacy by allowing users to investigate how infrared observations are processed and how genuine astronomical signals can be distinguished from instrumental artefacts and noise.

What makes Farlight distinctive is its emphasis on reliability rather than simply producing attractive astronomical images. The project incorporates validation using real observations, control fields, null tests, source injections, and comparisons with reference astrometric measurements. It explicitly considers false detections, correlated noise, image-registration errors, and residual artefacts around bright stars. The validation work demonstrates why uncertainty estimation and careful calibration are essential when interpreting astronomical difference images. Results are presented with their limitations rather than treating every detected candidate as an astronomical discovery.

The project was developed using Python for the scientific processing and backend, with FastAPI providing the web API and server. The frontend uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, including interactive image visualisation and charting. Scientific and data-processing libraries include NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, Reproject, S3FS, Matplotlib, and Pillow. SQLite is used for application data storage, while Docker and Render support deployment.

The development process prioritised scientific reproducibility, data provenance, computational efficiency, accessibility, and transparent communication of uncertainty. Farlight aims to make publicly available space-telescope observations more approachable, encourage public engagement with astronomy, and provide an extensible foundation for exploring time-domain infrared observations and potential changes in the universe.
